Rejoicing in Snow at Lingjiang (with a Preface)
South of the Ranges there has been no snow since ancient times. In the twelfth month of the guimao year I chanced to pass through Lingjiang; at the sight of it I rejoiced and recorded it.
To the Chan Monk Kongjian on Quiescence
Summoned from Caoxi, Returning to the Garrison

I yield my form to the great transformation's law;
To go or stay, why should the heart decide?
Even if driven to the burning sea,
It is as though in the jewel grove I bide.
This stolen life has roots that shallow lie;
Tracks blotted out, the Way's source deepens on.
I strain my gaze across the cold sky's blue:
Floating clouds, from old days to the new.
Climbing the Mingchang Pagoda on Qiongzhou

In the Summer of the Bingwu Year, Begging My Way from Caoxi over the Ranges to Qianzhou, I Fell Ill from the Heat and Lodged at General Chen Wenji's Pond Pavilion; Watching Fish Sport in the Fresh Water, Apes Cry to the Moon, and Cranes and Deer Draw Near to Man as in Deep Mountains, We Sat Together at Night and, Moved in Heart, I Wrote Five Poems

Old, I am driven by an idle mind;
Born, I am driven by the force of karma.
In vain three inches of breath must link
A hundred years of this poor body's frame.
Medicine is not fate, nor stone a cure;
To fast the mind — is that a foolish thing?
I grieve only at the world's bitterness:
I would be a slave in the Buddha's house.

Lotus Temple
After Rain at Lingjiang, Loosing the Boat to Return to the Mountains: Two Poems
Guoshen Temple at Wujing

The mountain market gathers by the cloud;
The flowered temple opens by the stream.
To tame the living, never idle long,
I take my staff and chance to wander here.
My meal awaits the faithful donor's gift;
The lotus must the guild's own master plant.
This is, in truth, a pure and quiet ground —
Fit place to raise a sutra-preaching stand.
Returning Late from Begging
On the Day of the Buddha's Enlightenment

Tonight the morning star climbs up the sky —
The very hour that first dream woke from sleep.
The Snowy Mountain still stands in my eyes;
The bodhi tree still hangs its branches down.
Far off I think of hunger's wasting thin;
I call to mind the milk-rice that was given.
Six years of cold that pierced him to the bone —
Who knows the bitterness his heart has known?

Lodging at Yingzhou

I laugh at myself: what am I about,
Restless and weary, asking for the ford?
Just feel these three inches of breathing air —
Can they tie down a hundred years of body?
The whole wide earth is full of wandering guests;
This toiling life is gathered dust at last.
Look up, I pray, at the moon above the river —
How many men has all its shining passed?
Bitter Rain on a Spring Day: Two Poems

On burning frontiers cold and heat abound;
We look to this sweet season for relief.
Alas, the rain that falls from night to night
Has cut off all the spring and left us grief.
It breaks with ease a dream of pass and hill;
It lies most hard on him who roams afar.
Peach bloom and the third month's swelling stream —
Since ancient days, the place where fords are lost.

Venerating the Patriarch at De Mountain: Four Poems

The master held the Empty King's own seal;
I come, ashamed to be so late in years.
I gaze far back across a thousand years,
And still one single lamp hangs in the air.
Bird-cries are words before a word is spoken;
The mountain's light is Chan beyond all measure.
Within his hand a bar of raw, cold iron —
He scraped away the wild fox's slaver there.

All subtle, clinging views I cast away,
And come to study the ancient master's way.
His staff knocked on the lion's very bones;
His tongue put forth the utpala's blue flower.
His shining marks contain the autumn moon;
His spirit shrine lies hid in evening cloud.
Within that room, a ten-foot square of ground —
How many dragons and snakes has it seen through?

Before the hall I idly hold my bowl;
The lion slowly trains its cub at play.
The point where, face to face, you cannot turn;
The hour of bowing low and saying naught.
The final word I still have not made clear —
And so I doubt it even to this day.
I ask about the business of three years:
How could he know so early, and so well?
Mountain Dwelling: Ten Poems

Heaven and earth still keep my Way alive;
As I grow old, the hills and woods grow dear.
At leisure I open up the blue-eyed gaze —
One look, and all the world is yellow dust.
Glad I have won a mind that knows no birth;
I wear away this body full of outflows.
How many follow after phantom shadows —
All, all are people coming and people going.

This life by nature has nowhere to abide;
The flowing light can never be held fast.
Who will take the new sun and the new moon
And trade them for a face from long ago?
Sitting alone, I hear the birds and nothing;
I open the door and see only the hills.
When phantom conditions all have come to rest,
Why should I seek for leisure anywhere?

In the world's stir I often feel disgust;
Returning to the hills, my thoughts grow still.
Who ever laid a plan for a thousand years?
For one man's sake alone I linger here.
Vast and void, it comes to an empty kalpa;
Drop by drop, the great rivers gather up.
Only behold the principle of the pure:
This body and this world are always floating.

This nature is from the first unattached —
And why, then, is it not entirely free?
Only because of grasping and control
Is it swept on by the world's ceaseless flow.
We do not know the shade of empty flowers —
Pitiful foam upon the mighty sea.
Just open wide the pure and stainless eye,
And clearly see the tip of a single hair.

To wave the whisk was always my affair;
This idle heart — what can it do with sloth?
For now I take the strength of diligence
And tame and conquer the demon of sleep.
In silence the heavenly music blows;
In slow procession the water's waves go by.
There never was a single word at all —
Vimalakīrti should not wonder why.
Taking Leave of the Southern Marchmount

I go with mist and cloud about my face;
I walk with secret shame in every pace.
Only to render an old promise due —
Not chasing floating fame, as others do.

Let ape and crane not chide me for the parting;
The wind in the pines keeps its endless sound.
I leave behind one broad and lengthy tongue
To preach the unborn, day and night, around.
Traveling by Boat
Setting Out from Xiangtan at Dawn
Borrowed-Wind Pavilion

Heaven's course moved the blazing Han's decree;
All raced and chased the deer that autumn day.
Who would have thought a cloud-reclining guest
Would lend a chopstick to the plan's array?
The empire's rule was settled into three;
One fire repaid his hero's heart at last.
The east wind's grief runs down a thousand years —
The Jiang and Han's long waters flowing past.
